With poder you also ask for permission or a favour: “¿Puedo salir a las dos?”, “¿Puedes reservar el hotel?”. With querer you invite: “¿Quieres venir a la playa?”.
Laura has little money: she cannot pay for an expensive hotel.
For the flight, Gabriel has to bring his ID card.
Laura talks to her boss: “Can I leave early on Friday?”
Laura wants to go to the islands.
Laura is going to go to the islands on Saturday.
I don’t want to pay for the boat.
I can’t pay for the boat.
I don’t have to pay for the boat today.
“No tengo que” means it is not necessary. To say that something is impossible or not allowed, use “no puedo”: “I can’t take much water on the plane”.
Monday is a public holiday: Laura doesn’t have to work.
“Gabriel quiere ir a la playa” means…
Laura has no money for the boat. She says: “I can’t go to the islands”.
Which one is correct?
Julio, I need help. Gabriel and I want to travel to Cartagena on the long weekend.
Great! When can you leave?
I can leave on Friday morning, but Gabriel has to work until two.
Then you have to take the six p.m. flight. And how much money can you spend?
Not much. We can only pay for a small hotel. But I want to see the Rosario Islands!
Hmm… The boat to the islands is expensive. And for the boat, you have to book this week.
This week? I can’t decide today: I have to talk to Gabriel.
Of course. Some good news: you don’t have to come back on Sunday. Monday is a public holiday.
Perfect! Then on Sunday we can go to the beach all day.
Yes. And on Monday morning you are going to fly back to Bogotá on the eleven o’clock flight.
Thanks, Julio. I’ll talk to Gabriel tonight. I want to go to the islands!
Why can’t they take a flight on Friday morning?
Why doesn’t Laura decide about the islands today?
Do they have to come back on Sunday?
Mrs Ríos, can I leave at two on Friday?
Yes, you can leave at two.
Do you want to go to the islands on Saturday?
Laura and Gabriel have to book the hotel today.
We cannot spend much money.
I want to see the islands.
Can you book the hotel?
We can’t pay for an expensive hotel.
Why does Julio send the message?
When can they pay for the hotel?
By when do they have to book the boat?
What time do they have to be at the airport?
What does Laura have to bring?
want to
can / can’t
have to · don’t have to
Conjugated verb + infinitive. Querer and poder go straight to the infinitive; tener needs “que”. And careful: “no puedo” = impossible; “no tengo que” = not necessary.
On Friday Gabriel has to work until two.
Laura really likes the sea: she wants to see the islands.
I have no money: I can’t pay for the boat.
Can you all travel on Monday?
Tomorrow is a holiday: I don’t have to go to the office. Great!
Sara, a colleague of Laura’s, also wants to travel: to Medellín, with her mother. Write one sentence for each idea.

You can now say what you want, can and have to do with a verb + infinitive. In class 041 you meet another two-verb combination: estar + gerund, to say what you are doing right now. “I am booking the hotel right now”.
It is Saturday, six in the evening. Sofía calls her friend Pablo: “What are you doing?”. Pablo answers: “I am cooking right now”. Today you learn to say what is happening at this moment.
I work every day, Monday to Friday.
I am not working today. Right now I am cooking.
“Ahora estoy cocinando” is about…
“Trabajo todos los días” is about…
Sofía asks about this moment. What does she say?
to be + -ing: what is happening now
I am cooking a soup now.
Mario is listening to the radio.
Sofía and her friends are waiting at the cinema.
What are you doing, Pablo?
Irene and Pablo are cooking.
Which piece changes with the person?
To make the gerund, take off -ar, -er or -ir and add -ando or -iendo. There are only two endings.
“Le + iendo” is written leyendo: an i between two vowels becomes y. “Dormir” changes o to u: durmiendo.
to speak → speaking
to drink → drinking
to read → reading
to sleep → sleeping
Sometimes people use the present for now: “¿Qué haces?” — “Cocino”. That is correct. But to say clearly that the action is in progress, use estar + gerund: “Estoy cocinando”.
On Saturdays Pablo rests at home.
Shh… Irene is sleeping right now.
Irene works at night at the hospital. She is a nurse.
I am listening to the radio now.
We are eating.
Hi, Pablo! What are you doing?
Hi, Sofía. Right now I am cooking a vegetable soup.
Yum! Aren’t you working today?
No. I work Monday to Friday. On Saturdays I rest.
And Irene? Is she at home?
Yes, but she is sleeping. She works nights at the hospital.
Oh, of course. I can hear another voice. Who is talking?
It is the radio. My brother Mario is reading on the sofa and listening to the football.
Listen, Lucas, Ana and I are going to the cinema at eight. Are you coming?
I can’t today, sorry. My parents are coming for dinner at eight.
OK, another day. Enjoy your meal!
What is Pablo doing?
Why is Irene sleeping?
What is Mario doing?
I am making rice for my parents now.
Irene is sleeping in her room.
Mario is reading a novel.
Sofía, Lucas and Ana are waiting in line.
And you, Sofía? What are you doing now?
Irene is sleeping now.
Mario is reading a book.
We are watching the film.
I work every day, but today I am resting.
Where is Sofía?
What is Sofía doing?
What is Lucas doing?
What is the weather like?
What time does the film start today?
to be + -ing: happening now
present: what you usually do
two special forms to remember

Two pieces, always: estar conjugated + gerund (-ando, -iendo). Only estar changes; the gerund never does. Routine goes in the present: “Trabajo todos los días”; what is happening now goes with estar + gerund: “Estoy trabajando ahora”.
Shh… the neighbours’ baby is sleeping.
Right now Ana and I are having a coffee.
Lucas works in an office every day.
What are you reading now?
My friends are eating in a restaurant.
It is Monday morning. Pablo is at work and his boss, Elena, phones: “What is everyone doing?”. Write Pablo’s answers.

You can now say what you are doing: “Estoy cocinando la sopa”. In class 042 you learn not to repeat those things, with lo, la, los, las: “¿La sopa? La estoy cocinando”. It is the natural next step to speak more fluently.

It is Monday morning at a small design company. Marta, the coordinator, finds a note from her boss, Elena: “Ana buys bread today”. On Friday there is a lunch with clients at the office, and the team needs to know who does what and when.
Ana buys bread today.
What does Ana buy?
Ana does not buy cheese.
“Ana compra pan hoy” is…
“¿Qué compra Ana?” asks about…
In “Ana no compra queso”, “no” goes…
Who does what, and when?
Elena is away on a trip this week.
Marta and Elena work at a design company.
I buy the coffee on Mondays.
Ana buys bread today. = Today Ana buys bread.
Ana calls Diego. ≠ Diego calls Ana.
In “Ana llama a Diego”, Ana does the action and Diego receives it. The person after “a” receives the call.
“Hoy Ana compra pan” means…
“Diego llama a Ana”: who is calling?
Today Elena and Ana make the coffee.
Yes / no, or a piece of information?
Is Ana buying bread today? — Yes.
The same question: the verb can also go first.
What does Ana buy? — Bread.
Who buys bread? — Ana.
When does Ana buy bread? — Today.
Who buys bread?
When does Ana buy bread?
In a yes / no question, your voice goes up at the end. In a statement, it goes down. In writing, Spanish uses two marks: ¿ at the start and ? at the end.
Marta wants to know the person. What does she ask?
Which one is correct?
“¿Ana compra pan hoy?” A possible answer:
Where does “no” go?
Today Elena is not working at the office: she is away.
The cheese? Ana does not buy it.
“Is Ana buying cheese?” “No, she isn’t buying cheese.”
Elena is not working this week.
The bread? Ana is not buying it tomorrow: she is buying it today.
“Is Elena at the office?” “No, she isn’t.”
Good morning, team. There is a note from Elena, but it has a coffee stain. Who is calling the restaurant on Wednesday?
Me. Elena isn’t here this week, so I’m calling the restaurant.
Thanks, Diego. Ana, are you buying the bread today?
Yes, I’m buying the bread today. But I’m not buying the cheese.
The note says: “Lucía does not prepare the room”. So what do I prepare?
You prepare the drinks, Lucía. I prepare the room on Thursday.
Perfect. And the flowers? When is Raúl buying the flowers?
It isn’t clear. Is Raúl buying the flowers on Thursday or on Friday?
Not on Thursday. Raúl doesn’t work on Thursdays.
Then he buys them on Friday morning. Who is talking to Raúl today?
I’ll talk to him at eleven. See you later!
Who is calling the restaurant?
What does Marta prepare on Thursday?
Who is talking to Raúl today?
What does Marta ask?
When does Diego call the restaurant?
On Friday Raúl and Ana arrive early at the office.
“Does Raúl work on Thursdays?” “No, he doesn’t work on Thursdays.”
Raúl buys flowers on Friday.
Where do the clients eat?
Diego does not work on Monday.
What does Lucía prepare?
Why does Elena call?
When does Ana buy the bread?
Why does Raúl buy the flowers on Friday?
How many clients arrive on Friday?
What does Elena ask at the end?
statement: the time phrase can move, the meaning stays
question: yes / no, or a piece of information
negative: “no” right before the verb
First who, then the verb. In a question with qué, quién or cuándo, the verb comes right after the question word. And “no” always goes before the verb: “Ana no compra pan”, never “compra no”.
Diego does not work on Tuesday.
Who closes the office? — Marta.
What is Lucía preparing for the lunch?
On Friday the clients arrive at one.
Which one is written correctly?
It is Saturday. On Lucía’s fridge there is a note: “My brother cooks on Sunday”. Sara, her flatmate, does not quite understand the note and asks questions. Write Sara’s sentences.

You can now order a sentence, ask with qué, quién or cuándo, and say no with “no”. In class 044 you put all of A1 together (ser, estar, hay, articles, possessives) to describe a place and ask for useful information: “¿Dónde está tu habitación?”. It is the natural next step: using these sentences in a complete conversation.
